summary: How the thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes do their jobs: the thymus builds a safe T cell repertoire, the spleen filters blood, and lymph nodes bring naive lymphocytes together with antigen. The exam asks you to predict what happens when one of these organs is removed, fails, or is suppressed by cortisol.

points: Bone marrow T cell precursors enter the thymus near the corticomedullary junction and move to the outer cortex as double negative (CD4- CD8-) thymocytes.
They rearrange the TCR beta chain, then the alpha chain, and become double positive (CD4+ CD8+).
Positive selection (cortex): thymocytes that bind self MHC on cortical epithelial cells with modest affinity survive; the rest die by neglect.
Binding MHC class I makes a CD8 T cell; binding MHC class II makes a CD4 T cell.
Negative selection (medulla): thymocytes that bind self peptide-MHC too strongly die by apoptosis or become FOXP3+ regulatory T cells.
AIRE lets medullary epithelial cells express tissue antigens (insulin, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal proteins) so self-reactive cells can be deleted.
Most thymocytes never leave the thymus; only a small fraction exit as mature single positive naive T cells.
Red pulp (cords and sinusoids): rigid or aged red cells cannot squeeze through slits in the sinus wall, and macrophages eat them.
Pitting: splenic macrophages remove inclusions such as Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants) and Heinz bodies while the red cell survives.
White pulp: T cells in the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath, B cells in follicles.
Marginal zone B cells and macrophages trap blood-borne antigen and make fast IgM against bacterial polysaccharide capsules.
Splenic macrophages clear bacteria coated with IgG or C3b, which matters most for encapsulated bacteria.
About one third of the body's platelets are held in the spleen.
Blood smear: Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, and sometimes Heinz bodies and acanthocytes.
Thrombocytosis after splenectomy because the splenic platelet pool is gone.
Overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated bacteria: S pneumoniae, H influenzae type b, N meningitidis.
Sickle cell disease: repeated splenic infarcts cause functional asplenia in early childhood (autosplenectomy).

notes.h: Lymph nodes: where naive cells meet antigen
points: Naive T and B cells leave the blood through high endothelial venules (HEVs) in the paracortex.
L-selectin (CD62L) on the lymphocyte binds addressins on HEVs and slows it down.
CCR7 on the lymphocyte binds the chemokines CCL19 and CCL21, which activates integrins for firm arrest.
Dendritic cells pick up antigen in tissue, switch on CCR7, and travel in afferent lymph to the node.
Lymphocytes that find no antigen leave through efferent lymph, drawn out by sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P).
Activated effector T cells lose L-selectin and CCR7, so they home to inflamed tissue instead of nodes.
Lymphopenia: lymphocytes redistribute out of the blood and lymphocyte apoptosis increases.
Eosinopenia and fewer monocytes and basophils.
Neutrophilia: neutrophils demarginate from vessel walls (less adhesion), and marrow release rises.
Thymic atrophy and shrinkage of lymphoid tissue (stress involution of the thymus).
Seen with severe stress, Cushing syndrome, and glucocorticoid treatment.

tricks.label: Please SHiNE my SKiS
tricks.text: Encapsulated bacteria: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, S pneumoniae, H influenzae type b, N meningitidis, E coli, Salmonella, Klebsiella, group B Streptococcus. The big three after splenectomy are S pneumoniae, Hib, and N meningitidis.

tricks.label: Cortex first, medulla second
tricks.text: Thymocytes move from cortex to medulla, and selection follows the same order: first prove you can see self MHC (positive, cortex), then prove you do not attack self (negative, medulla).

tricks.label: Steroids lift neutrophils off the wall
tricks.text: Cortisol raises every count that depends on letting go of the vessel wall (neutrophils) and lowers the ones it pushes out of the blood or kills (lymphocytes, eosinophils).

highYield: Positive selection happens in the cortex on cortical epithelial MHC; negative selection happens in the medulla with AIRE.
Howell-Jolly bodies on a smear mean the spleen is absent or not working.
Asplenia raises the risk of fatal sepsis from S pneumoniae, Hib, and N meningitidis.
Sickle cell disease causes functional asplenia in early childhood through repeated splenic infarcts.
Naive lymphocytes enter nodes through HEVs using L-selectin and CCR7.
Cortisol causes neutrophilia, lymphopenia, eosinopenia, and thymic atrophy.
pitfalls: Positive selection is about MHC restriction (cortex); negative selection is about self tolerance (medulla). Do not swap the locations.
Neutrophilia from cortisol comes from demargination of cells already in vessels and from marrow release; it does not signal infection.
Thrombocytosis after splenectomy comes from losing the platelet pool; platelet production is not the main change.
Effector T cells lose L-selectin and CCR7; only naive and central memory cells home through HEVs.

MHC I binding gives CD8, MHC II binding gives CD4
Negative selection in the medulla on medullary epithelial and dendritic cells
AIRE drives tissue antigen expression in the medulla
Strong binders die or become FOXP3+ Tregs; mature naive T cells exit

Lost pitting leads to Howell-Jolly bodies and Heinz bodies

Lost macrophage clearance of opsonized bacteria

summary: Lymph is the fluid and protein that leak out of capillaries and are carried back to the blood through lymphatic vessels. The exam asks you to explain where lymph comes from, why it is the only way to return filtered protein, what moves it, and what happens when the vessels are damaged or missing.

points: Starling forces: capillary hydrostatic pressure and interstitial oncotic pressure push fluid out; plasma oncotic pressure pulls it back, and interstitial hydrostatic pressure opposes filtration only when it is positive.
Filtration out of capillaries is slightly greater than reabsorption into them.
The leftover fluid, about 2 to 3 L per day, enters lymphatic capillaries and becomes lymph.
Interstitial pressure is normally slightly negative in loose tissue (about -3 mmHg in subcutaneous tissue).
Interstitial fluid with electrolytes and glucose at about plasma levels.
Plasma protein that leaked out of capillaries; lymph protein ranges from about 2 g/dL (limbs) to about 6 g/dL (liver).
Lymphocytes, especially in efferent lymph leaving nodes.
Chyle: milky intestinal lymph full of chylomicrons after a fatty meal.
Lymph is the only route back to the blood for filtered protein, because protein cannot be reabsorbed into capillaries against its gradient.
Without lymph flow, interstitial protein builds up, interstitial oncotic pressure rises, and edema follows.
Lymphatic capillaries have overlapping endothelial flaps and anchoring filaments that open when tissue swells.
Collecting lymphatics are divided by one-way valves into segments (lymphangions).
Each lymphangion contracts on its own when stretched by filling (intrinsic smooth muscle pump).
External squeezing helps: skeletal muscle contraction, arterial pulsation, and body movement.
Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and draws thoracic duct lymph toward the left venous angle.
Rising interstitial pressure (from about -3 up to about 0 to +2 mmHg) can raise lymph flow about 20 fold before it levels off.
Edema from failed lymph drainage, so the fluid is protein rich.
Early lymphedema may pit; chronic protein-rich fluid causes fibrosis and fat deposition, so it becomes nonpitting.
Skin thickens, with peau d'orange and recurrent cellulitis.
Secondary causes: axillary node dissection or radiation for breast cancer, and Wuchereria bancrofti filariasis.
W bancrofti: mosquito-borne nematode whose adult worms live in lymphatics, causing elephantiasis and hydrocele.
Milroy disease: autosomal dominant FLT4 (VEGFR3) mutation, congenital lower limb lymphedema.
Turner syndrome (45,X): cystic hygroma of the neck in the fetus, webbed neck, and hand and foot lymphedema at birth.

rows: Venous obstruction, heart failure, volume overload
Protein leak (inflammation) or protein not removed (lymph block)
Normally slightly negative, so it favors filtration

charts.title: Causes of lymphedema
rows: Arm swelling on the treated side

tricks.label: Lymph is the protein return line
tricks.text: Capillaries can take water back but not protein. Anything that blocks lymph leaves protein behind, so lymphedema fluid is protein rich and the tissue scars.

tricks.label: Milroy, VEGF receptor 3
tricks.text: VEGF-C acting on VEGFR3 (the FLT4 gene product) builds lymphatic vessels. One mutant FLT4 copy (autosomal dominant) is enough to make the legs swell from birth.

tricks.label: Webbed neck is an old hygroma
tricks.text: In Turner syndrome the fetal jugular lymph sacs fail to drain, the neck balloons (cystic hygroma), and the stretched skin later leaves a webbed neck.

highYield: About 2 to 3 L of lymph returns to the blood each day.
Lymph is the only way filtered plasma protein gets back to the circulation.
Lymph flow rises steeply as interstitial pressure rises, which is a safety factor against edema.
Lymphedema is protein rich and turns nonpitting as fibrosis develops.
Milroy disease is an FLT4 (VEGFR3) mutation; Turner syndrome gives cystic hygroma.
W bancrofti adults block lymphatics and cause elephantiasis of legs and scrotum.
pitfalls: Heart failure and nephrotic edema are low-protein transudates; lymphedema is high protein. Protein content tells you the mechanism.
Interstitial pressure is normally slightly negative; it becomes positive only as edema builds.
Chyle is intestinal lymph with chylomicrons; a milky pleural effusion with high triglyceride is a chylothorax from a torn or blocked thoracic duct (trauma, surgery, lymphoma).
Cystic hygroma is linked to Turner syndrome (and other aneuploidies); Milroy disease is a single gene disorder with a normal karyotype.

l: Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, higher at the arterial end
Plasma oncotic pressure pulls fluid in
Interstitial oncotic pressure pulls fluid out
Interstitial hydrostatic pressure, slightly negative normally
Net filtration slightly exceeds reabsorption
Excess fluid and leaked protein enter the lymphatic capillary
About 2 to 3 L of lymph per day returns to the veins

dumps.p: Make a table of the forces that move lymph, then list four causes of lymphedema with the mechanism of each.
l: Intrinsic lymphangion contraction when stretched
One-way valves between lymphangions
Skeletal muscle pump and arterial pulsation
Inspiration lowers thoracic pressure and helps thoracic duct flow
Axillary dissection or radiation removes or scars drainage
W bancrofti adult worms block lymphatics
Milroy disease: FLT4 (VEGFR3) mutation, poor lymphatic development
Turner syndrome: cystic hygroma and congenital lymphedema

summary: The chemistry behind immune defense: how phagocytes make bleach, why one purine enzyme decides whether lymphocytes live, which arachidonic acid products drive inflammation, and how vitamins, minerals, and protein supply keep the immune system working. The exam turns each of these into a deficiency you have to predict.

points: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in the pentose phosphate pathway makes NADPH.
NADPH oxidase in the phagosome membrane uses NADPH to turn O2 into superoxide.
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
Myeloperoxidase (in neutrophil granules) combines H2O2 with chloride to make hypochlorous acid (HOCl, bleach).
Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD): NADPH oxidase defect, most often X-linked (CYBB, gp91phox), some autosomal recessive.
CGD phagocytes can still make HOCl if the microbe supplies its own H2O2.
Catalase-positive microbes destroy their own H2O2, so they survive: S aureus, Aspergillus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia, Nocardia.
Uncleared organisms are walled off in granulomas (lymph nodes, liver, lung, skin).
Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow test: normal cells fluoresce after stimulation; CGD cells show little or no fluorescence.
Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT): normal cells reduce the yellow dye to blue; CGD cells stay yellow.
Adenosine deaminase converts adenosine and deoxyadenosine to inosine and deoxyinosine in purine salvage.
Without ADA, deoxyadenosine builds up and lymphocytes phosphorylate it to dATP.
dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, so no deoxynucleotides are made for DNA.
Dividing lymphocytes die: T, B, and NK cells are all low (autosomal recessive SCID).
Phospholipase A2 frees arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids; glucocorticoids inhibit this step.
Cyclooxygenase (COX-1, COX-2) makes PGE2 (fever, pain, vasodilation), PGI2, and thromboxane A2.
Thromboxane A2 (platelets) causes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction; PGI2 (endothelium) does the opposite.
5-lipoxygenase makes LTB4, a strong neutrophil chemoattractant.
LTC4, LTD4, LTE4 (cysteinyl leukotrienes) cause bronchoconstriction and raise vascular permeability.
Granuloma macrophages in sarcoidosis express 1-alpha-hydroxylase that PTH does not control.
They convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol, which raises gut calcium absorption: hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, low PTH.
Toll-like receptor signals in macrophages induce the vitamin D receptor and 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
Calcitriol inside macrophages induces cathelicidin (LL-37), an antimicrobial peptide active against M tuberculosis.
Zinc deficiency: thymic atrophy, lymphopenia, poor T cell function, poor wound healing.
Acrodermatitis enteropathica: autosomal recessive defect of the intestinal zinc transporter ZIP4 (SLC39A4); rash around mouth, anus, and limbs, alopecia, diarrhea.
Vitamin A keeps mucosal epithelium differentiated; deficiency causes squamous metaplasia (keratinization) of airway, urinary, and conjunctival epithelium.
Vitamin A deficiency makes measles more severe and more often fatal.
Protein-energy malnutrition is the most common cause of acquired immunodeficiency worldwide.
Malnutrition shrinks the thymus and weakens cell-mediated immunity (poor delayed skin test responses, low CD4 counts).
Marasmus: calorie deficit with severe wasting and no edema. Kwashiorkor: protein deficit with edema, fatty liver, and skin changes.

charts.title: Phagocyte killing defects
rows: Often no symptoms; some Candida infections

charts.title: Nutrients and immune effects
rows: Thymic atrophy, poor T cell function
Acral and periorificial rash, alopecia, diarrhea, poor wound healing
Wasting; edema and fatty liver in kwashiorkor

tricks.label: Neutrophils arrive B4 others
tricks.text: LTB4 is the leukotriene that calls in neutrophils.

tricks.label: Kwashiorkor: a protein-deficient MEAL
tricks.text: Malnutrition, Edema, Anemia, Liver (fatty).

tricks.label: Borrowed peroxide
tricks.text: A CGD phagocyte can only make bleach with H2O2 the microbe hands it. Catalase-positive microbes destroy their own H2O2, so they are the ones that cause infections.

tricks.label: ADA: too much of one building block
tricks.text: Excess dATP shuts off ribonucleotide reductase, so the cell starves for all the other deoxynucleotides. Lymphocytes, which divide fast and trap dATP, die first.

highYield: CGD: NADPH oxidase defect, abnormal DHR test, infections with S aureus, Aspergillus, B cepacia, Serratia, Nocardia.
ADA deficiency: dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, giving SCID with T, B, and NK cells all low.
LTB4 calls neutrophils; LTC4, LTD4, LTE4 constrict bronchi and raise permeability; PGE2 causes fever.
Sarcoidosis hypercalcemia comes from unregulated macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase making calcitriol, with low PTH.
Acrodermatitis enteropathica is inherited zinc malabsorption with rash, alopecia, diarrhea, and infections.
Vitamin A deficiency increases measles severity and mortality.
Protein-energy malnutrition is the leading cause of immunodeficiency worldwide.
pitfalls: CGD has normal phagocytosis and normal myeloperoxidase; only the oxidative burst fails.
MPO deficiency leaves the NBT test normal, because superoxide is still made.
Sarcoidosis hypercalcemia has low PTH and high calcitriol; primary hyperparathyroidism has high PTH.
Kwashiorkor has edema from low albumin; marasmus has wasting without edema.
Glucocorticoids block phospholipase A2 (both COX and LOX products fall); NSAIDs block only COX.

CGD: NADPH oxidase missing, usually X-linked
Catalase-positive organisms remove their own H2O2 and survive

COX branch to PGH2
PGE2: fever, pain, vasodilation

summary: The biochemistry of what lymph carries: dietary fat packaged as chylomicrons that travel through the lymph before reaching the blood, and plasma protein that leaks out of capillaries at different rates in different organs. The exam asks you to follow a chylomicron from the gut to the liver and to predict what happens when one step is missing.

points: Enterocytes take up 2-monoglyceride and free fatty acids from micelles.
Smooth ER enzymes re-esterify them into triglyceride.
ApoB-48 comes from the apoB gene; intestinal mRNA editing creates an early stop codon, so the protein is about 48% of apoB-100.
Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) loads triglyceride onto apoB-48 in the ER.
The chylomicron passes through the Golgi and is released from the basolateral side.
Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries, so they enter lacteals (lymphatic capillaries in the villi).
They travel through the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct and enter the blood at the left venous angle.
This route bypasses the liver, so dietary fat reaches muscle and adipose tissue first.
Short and medium chain fatty acids skip chylomicrons and go straight to portal blood.
Intestinal lymph full of chylomicrons is milky (chyle).
In the blood, HDL hands the chylomicron apoC-II and apoE.
ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase (LPL) on capillary endothelium of adipose tissue, muscle, and heart.
LPL frees fatty acids: muscle oxidizes them, adipose tissue stores them as triglyceride. Glycerol goes to the liver.
Insulin raises adipose LPL after a meal.
The smaller remnant keeps apoE and is taken up by the liver through apoE binding to hepatic receptors (LDL receptor and LRP1).
LPL or apoC-II deficiency: chylomicrons stay in plasma (very high triglyceride, pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas).
Autosomal recessive loss of MTP.
No apoB-48 or apoB-100 lipoproteins: chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL are absent; plasma triglyceride and cholesterol are very low.
Fat stays trapped in enterocytes (lipid-laden, foamy cells on biopsy) and steatorrhea starts in infancy.
Altered red cell membrane lipids produce acanthocytes.
Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, mostly vitamin E: spinocerebellar ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa.

notes.h: Why lymph protein differs by organ
points: Liver sinusoids are discontinuous with gaps and little basement membrane, so plasma protein leaks freely; hepatic lymph protein is about 6 g/dL.
Intestinal capillaries are fenestrated; intestinal lymph protein is about 3 to 4 g/dL.
Skeletal muscle capillaries are continuous with tight junctions; lymph protein is about 2 g/dL.
Liver and gut supply most of the protein in thoracic duct lymph.

charts.title: A chylomicron from start to finish
rows: Chylothorax if the thoracic duct is cut
Capillary endothelium of muscle and fat

tricks.label: 48 means gut, 100 means liver
tricks.text: ApoB-48 is the short, edited intestinal form on chylomicrons. ApoB-100 is the full liver form on VLDL and LDL. MTP is needed for both, which is why abetalipoproteinemia removes all of them.

tricks.label: C-II cuts, E eats
tricks.text: ApoC-II turns on lipoprotein lipase to cut triglyceride; apoE is the tag the liver uses to eat the remnant.

tricks.label: Leaky wall, rich lymph
tricks.text: The leakier the capillary wall, the more protein in the lymph: sinusoid beats fenestrated beats continuous.

highYield: Chylomicrons enter lacteals and the thoracic duct, reaching the blood without passing through the liver.
MTP loads triglyceride onto apoB-48; apoB-48 comes from mRNA editing of the apoB transcript.
ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase; apoE directs remnant uptake by the liver.
Abetalipoproteinemia: steatorrhea, acanthocytes, very low lipids, and vitamin E deficiency with ataxia.
Hepatic lymph has the most protein because liver sinusoids are discontinuous.
Medium chain fatty acids bypass the lymph and go to portal blood.
pitfalls: Abetalipoproteinemia removes chylomicrons and VLDL and LDL; LPL or apoC-II deficiency raises chylomicrons. Opposite plasma pictures.
LPL works on the capillary surface; hormone-sensitive lipase works inside fat cells. Do not swap them.
ApoB-48 and apoB-100 come from the same gene; the difference is RNA editing, not alternative genes.
Muscle lymph protein is low because muscle capillaries are continuous; low lymph protein there is normal.

dumps.p: Draw an enterocyte, a lacteal, the thoracic duct, a muscle capillary, and the liver. Trace a dietary triglyceride from the gut lumen to the liver and label each protein that acts on it.
l: Micelles deliver 2-monoglyceride and fatty acids to the enterocyte
Smooth ER re-esterifies triglyceride
MTP loads it onto apoB-48
Chylomicron enters the lacteal, not the portal blood
Thoracic duct carries it to the left venous angle
HDL donates apoC-II and apoE
ApoC-II activates LPL on muscle and adipose capillaries
ApoE-tagged remnant taken up by the liver

dumps.p: A 9-month-old has fatty stools and poor growth. Make a flowchart from the missing protein to every lab and clinical finding you would expect.
l: MTP missing (autosomal recessive)
No chylomicrons, VLDL, or LDL
Very low plasma triglyceride and cholesterol
Lipid-laden enterocytes on biopsy
Steatorrhea and failure to thrive
Acanthocytes on the smear
Vitamin E deficiency with ataxia and retinal degeneration

summary: The genes that build and control lymphocytes: the recombination machinery that makes antigen receptors, the cytokine and signaling genes behind each type of SCID, and the genes that enforce tolerance. The exam gives you a lymphocyte count, an immunoglobulin pattern, or a pedigree and asks which gene is broken.

points: RAG1 and RAG2 cut DNA at recombination signal sequences next to V, D, and J segments.
Heavy chain and TCR beta use V, D, and J; light chains and TCR alpha use V and J.
Nonhomologous end joining repairs the cuts (Artemis opens the hairpin ends).
TdT adds random N nucleotides at the joints, giving junctional diversity.
RAG deficiency: no receptors, so no T or B cells; NK cells need no rearranged receptor and are preserved.
X-linked SCID: IL2RG mutation in the common gamma chain shared by IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21 receptors.
No IL-7 signal means no T cells; no IL-15 signal means no NK cells; B cells are present but cannot work without T cell help.
JAK3 deficiency (autosomal recessive) copies the X-linked SCID profile because JAK3 signals for the common gamma chain.
ADA deficiency: T, B, and NK cells all absent.
T cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) are DNA circles cut out during TCR rearrangement; low TRECs on newborn screening flag SCID.
All SCID: absent thymic shadow, thrush, chronic diarrhea, Pneumocystis pneumonia, and danger from live vaccines.
X-linked recessive mutation in WAS, which encodes WASp, an actin cytoskeleton regulator in blood cells.
Thrombocytopenia with small platelets, eczema, and recurrent infections.
Immunoglobulins: low IgM, high IgA and IgE, IgG often normal.
Higher risk of autoimmunity and B cell lymphoma.
Carrier mother and unaffected father: each son has a 50% chance of being affected; each daughter a 50% chance of being a carrier.
Most common form: X-linked CD40 ligand (CD154) deficiency on activated CD4 T cells.
CD40L binding CD40 on B cells drives class switching and germinal center formation.
Result: normal or high IgM with low IgG, IgA, and IgE.
CD40L also activates macrophages and dendritic cells, so cell-mediated defense is weak too.
Infections: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, Cryptosporidium diarrhea, and recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections.
AIRE (autosomal recessive): failed thymic negative selection causes autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APS-1).
APS-1 classic triad: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency.
FOXP3 (X-linked) is the master transcription factor of regulatory T cells.
FOXP3 loss causes IPEX: immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy (neonatal type 1 diabetes, thyroiditis), enteropathy with severe diarrhea, X-linked.
Fas (CD95) on activated lymphocytes binds Fas ligand and triggers caspase 8, then executioner caspases (extrinsic apoptosis).
This ends clonal expansion after an infection and deletes self-reactive lymphocytes in the periphery.
Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS), usually from FAS mutation: chronic lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias.
ALPS labs: more CD4- CD8- (double negative) alpha-beta T cells in blood; higher lymphoma risk.

charts.title: SCID by gene
rows: No signal from common gamma chain

charts.title: Inherited immune disorders and their immunoglobulins
rows: Low IgM, high IgA and IgE
High or normal IgM; low IgG, IgA, IgE

tricks.label: WATER
tricks.text: Wiskott-Aldrich: Thrombocytopenia, Eczema, Recurrent infections.

tricks.label: NK cells tell you the gene
tricks.text: In SCID, NK cells present means RAG (they need no rearranged receptor). NK cells absent with B cells present means the common gamma chain or JAK3. Everything absent means ADA.

tricks.label: Stuck on M
tricks.text: Hyper-IgM: B cells make IgM first and need CD40L from T cells to switch. No CD40L, no switch, so IgM is the only antibody left.

tricks.label: AIRE in the medulla, FOXP3 in the periphery
tricks.text: AIRE failure lets self-reactive T cells escape the thymus (central tolerance). FOXP3 failure means there are no Tregs to hold them back afterward (peripheral tolerance).

highYield: RAG deficiency: T and B cells absent, NK cells present.
X-linked SCID (IL2RG): T and NK absent, B cells present but nonfunctional.
Low TRECs on newborn screening point to SCID.
Wiskott-Aldrich: small platelets, eczema, infections, low IgM, high IgA and IgE, X-linked.
CD40L deficiency: high IgM, low other isotypes, Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium infections.
AIRE mutation: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, Addison disease.
FAS mutation (ALPS): lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, double negative T cells.
pitfalls: Wiskott-Aldrich platelets are small; immune thrombocytopenia and Bernard-Soulier platelets are normal sized or large.
Hyper-IgM patients have normal or high IgM but almost no IgG, so they lack the IgG that opsonizes and neutralizes.
X-linked SCID boys have B cells on flow cytometry; the B cells are present but cannot make useful antibody without T cell help.
In an X-linked pedigree, an affected father passes the gene to all daughters (carriers) and to none of his sons.
ALPS is lymphoproliferative but not malignant at first; the big nodes come from failed apoptosis.

dumps.p: Build a table on blank paper for four SCID genes. For each, list the inheritance, which lymphocytes are present or absent, and the mechanism.
l: IL2RG: X-linked, T and NK absent, B present
Common gamma chain is shared by IL-2, 4, 7, 9, 15, 21 receptors
JAK3: autosomal recessive, same profile as IL2RG
ADA: autosomal recessive, all three absent, dATP toxicity
RAG1 or RAG2: autosomal recessive, T and B absent, NK present
RAG needed for V(D)J recombination
Low TRECs on newborn screening in all

summary: How the immune system gets switched on by microbes, tumors, and vaccines, and how it turns against the body in autoimmunity and hypersensitivity. These are the core rules the exam uses to explain almost every immune disease, so expect to classify reactions and predict what blocking a signal will do.

points: Innate: germline-encoded pattern recognition receptors (Toll-like receptors, NOD-like receptors) detect microbial patterns.
Examples: TLR4 senses LPS, TLR5 senses flagellin, TLR3 senses dsRNA, TLR9 senses unmethylated CpG DNA.
Innate cells and proteins: neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells, dendritic cells, complement. Response in minutes to hours, no memory.
Adaptive: T and B cells with rearranged receptors, clonal expansion over days, and memory.
Innate signals (cytokines, B7 on dendritic cells) are needed to start an adaptive response.
Signal 1: the TCR binds a peptide on MHC (CD4 with class II, CD8 with class I).
Signal 2: CD28 on the T cell binds B7 (CD80 or CD86) on the antigen-presenting cell.
Signal 1 without signal 2 leads to anergy, a key form of peripheral tolerance.
CTLA-4 binds B7 more tightly than CD28 does and shuts activation down; Tregs express it constantly.
PD-1 on activated T cells binds PD-L1 or PD-L2 and dampens T cell signaling.
Antibodies that block CTLA-4 or PD-1 release this brake, boosting antitumor T cells and causing autoimmune side effects.
Tumor antigens include mutated proteins (neoantigens), viral oncoproteins (HPV E6 and E7), and overexpressed self proteins.
Dendritic cells cross-present tumor antigen to prime CD8 T cells; CD8 T cells kill tumor cells showing it on MHC class I.
NK cells kill cells that lose MHC class I (missing self) or express stress ligands.
Escape: loss of MHC class I or beta-2 microglobulin hides tumors from CD8 T cells.
Escape: PD-L1 on tumor cells switches off PD-1+ T cells; tumors also recruit Tregs and secrete TGF-beta.
Live attenuated (MMR, varicella, yellow fever): replicate, give strong cellular and humoral immunity, often lifelong.
Live vaccines are avoided in severe immunodeficiency and in pregnancy.
Inactivated (rabies, hepatitis A, injected polio, injected influenza): mostly antibody, need boosters.
Subunit or recombinant (hepatitis B surface antigen, HPV): a single protein, safe in immunodeficiency.
Toxoid (tetanus, diphtheria): inactivated toxin that raises neutralizing antibody.
Conjugate (Hib, pneumococcal, meningococcal): capsule linked to a protein carrier turns a T-independent response into a T-dependent one, so infants under 2 years respond and form memory.
Failed central tolerance: self-reactive cells escape thymic negative selection (AIRE defects).
Failed peripheral tolerance: lost anergy, Treg failure (FOXP3), or lost Fas-mediated deletion.
HLA susceptibility: HLA-B27 (ankylosing spondylitis), HLA-DR3 and DR4 (type 1 diabetes), HLA-DR4 (rheumatoid arthritis), HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 (celiac disease).
Molecular mimicry: group A strep M protein cross-reacts with cardiac myosin and valve tissue, causing rheumatic fever.
Molecular mimicry: Campylobacter jejuni lipooligosaccharide resembles nerve gangliosides, causing Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Type I: IgE on mast cells cross-linked by antigen; histamine and leukotrienes within minutes.
Type II: IgG or IgM bind antigens on cells or matrix; complement, phagocytosis, or receptor blocking or stimulation.
Type III: antigen-antibody complexes deposit in vessels, glomeruli, and joints; complement and neutrophils damage tissue; low C3.
Type IV: T cells, no antibody; CD4 Th1 cells activate macrophages or CD8 cells kill directly; peaks at 48 to 72 hours.

tricks.label: Is there antibody, and where is the antigen?
tricks.text: No antibody means type IV. IgE means type I. Antibody against something fixed on a cell or membrane means type II. Antibody bound to free antigen that lands somewhere else means type III.

highYield: T cell activation needs TCR plus MHC (signal 1) and CD28 plus B7 (signal 2); signal 1 alone gives anergy.
CTLA-4 and PD-1 are inhibitory checkpoints that tumors exploit.
NK cells kill tumor cells that lose MHC class I.
Live attenuated vaccines give the strongest immunity but are avoided in immunodeficiency and pregnancy.
Conjugate vaccines make polysaccharide responses T-dependent, so infants respond.
Rheumatic fever: M protein mimicry; Guillain-Barre: C jejuni ganglioside mimicry.
Type III disease lowers complement (C3); type IV involves no antibody.
pitfalls: Rheumatic fever and Goodpasture syndrome are type II; poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is type III. Same organism can cause different types.
Contact dermatitis (poison ivy, nickel) is type IV; latex hives or anaphylaxis are type I.
CTLA-4 and CD28 bind the same ligand (B7); CTLA-4 inhibits, CD28 activates.
Losing MHC class I protects a tumor from CD8 T cells but makes it a target for NK cells.
Pure polysaccharide vaccines work poorly before age 2; the conjugate form fixes this.

summary: The microbiology of the systemic infections in this system: parvovirus B19, Haemophilus influenzae type b, influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, EBV, HHV-6 and HHV-7, group A strep, and Toxoplasma. The exam expects you to link each organism's structure, receptor, spread, and virulence factors to the disease it causes.

points: Small, nonenveloped, single-stranded DNA virus; needs dividing cells to replicate.
Binds P antigen (globoside) on erythroid progenitors, which it infects and kills.
Red cell production stops for about a week (reticulocytopenia); healthy people barely notice because red cells live about 120 days.
Chronic hemolysis (sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis): transient aplastic crisis.
Spread by respiratory droplets, blood products, and across the placenta; fetal infection can cause severe anemia and hydrops fetalis.
The slapped cheek rash of fifth disease appears with the antibody response, after the infectious phase.
Small gram-negative coccobacillus spread by respiratory droplets.
Polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP) capsule is the main virulence factor; it resists phagocytosis and complement.
IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA and helps colonization.
Grows on chocolate agar, which supplies factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD+).
Causes meningitis, epiglottitis, pneumonia, and septic arthritis in unvaccinated children; the vaccine is PRP conjugated to a protein.
Orthomyxovirus: enveloped, segmented, negative-sense single-stranded RNA (8 segments in influenza A).
Hemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory epithelium and drives membrane fusion.
Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid so new virions can leave the cell.
Antigenic drift: point mutations in HA and NA cause yearly epidemics.
Antigenic shift: two strains swap gene segments (reassortment) to make a new HA or NA subtype; pandemics, influenza A only.
Measles and mumps are paramyxoviruses: enveloped, nonsegmented, negative-sense single-stranded RNA.
Their F (fusion) protein fuses cells into syncytia; measles makes Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells in lymphoid tissue.
Measles: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, rash spreading head to toe; pneumonia and encephalitis are the dangerous complications.
Mumps: parotitis, orchitis, and aseptic meningitis.
Rubella: enveloped positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus (formerly classed as a togavirus); mild rash and postauricular lymphadenopathy.
All three spread by respiratory droplets; measles is also airborne and extremely contagious.
Herpesviruses: enveloped, double-stranded DNA, lifelong latency; spread by saliva.
EBV enters B cells through CD21 (complement receptor 2) and stays latent in memory B cells.
Atypical lymphocytes in mononucleosis are reactive CD8 T cells; heterophile antibodies come from polyclonal B cell activation.
HHV-6 and HHV-7 infect CD4 T cells and cause roseola infantum: high fever for days, then rash as the fever breaks.
Gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase-negative, beta-hemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive.
M protein blocks phagocytosis and complement deposition; it is also the mimicry antigen in rheumatic fever.
Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins are superantigens: they link MHC class II to the TCR beta chain outside the peptide groove and activate huge numbers of T cells.
Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor, later desquamation; superantigens can also cause streptococcal toxic shock.
Obligate intracellular protozoan; the cat is the definitive host where the sexual stage occurs in the gut.
Cats shed oocysts in feces; they become infectious after 1 to 5 days in the environment.
Humans are infected by sporulated oocysts (soil, litter, produce) or by tissue cysts with bradyzoites in undercooked meat.
Tachyzoites multiply fast and spread; immunity forces them into tissue cysts (bradyzoites) in brain, muscle, and retina.
Primary infection in pregnancy: tachyzoites cross the placenta, causing chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications.

tricks.label: Shift needs a swap
tricks.text: Only a segmented genome can trade whole genes. Influenza A has animal hosts that carry other subtypes, so it alone can shift.

highYield: Parvovirus B19 binds P antigen on erythroid progenitors: aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemia, hydrops fetalis in the fetus.
Hib PRP capsule is the main virulence factor and the target of the conjugate vaccine.
Influenza hemagglutinin binds sialic acid; neuraminidase releases virions; shift by reassortment causes pandemics.
Measles F protein forms Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells.
EBV enters B cells through CD21; the atypical lymphocytes are CD8 T cells.
Group A strep pyrogenic exotoxins are superantigens that cause scarlet fever.
Toxoplasma: cat is the definitive host; humans get oocysts from cat feces or tissue cysts from undercooked meat.
pitfalls: Parvovirus B19 is the only DNA virus here that is single-stranded; herpesviruses are double-stranded.
Measles and mumps are negative-sense; rubella is positive-sense. Do not group rubella with the paramyxoviruses.
Atypical lymphocytes in mono are T cells reacting to infected B cells; EBV itself infects the B cells.
Group A strep is bacitracin-sensitive and group B is resistant; both are beta-hemolytic.
Fresh cat feces are not yet infectious; oocysts need 1 to 5 days to sporulate.
